doc.title: Arturo Sandoval interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2023

title: What goes through his mind improvising; first hearing Dizzy and Bird
summary: He recounts Cuban village bands, strict classical school, and hearing a Gillespie-Parker compilation at about 18, which set him on a lifelong mission to learn.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Let me ask you about your improvising. I ask this question fairly often — what’s going on in your head. We were just talking about the brain and soul and can you describe

what’s going on in your head when you’re — like I was watching one of the many recordings or videos of your “Funky Cha-Cha.” And you’re playing these very intense bebop lines and so forth and I’m wondering what’s going on up there?

You know let’s rewind sixty years and I’m going to tell you — I started in my village, because I grew up in the village in the countryside of the island. I started playing traditional Cuban music with local bands, that was the first thing. And then I went to school later on to get classical training and I spent three years in that school, strictly classical. In that school, that was funny, we weren’t allowed to play, talk or listen to anything but classical music. It was like a military kind of thing. And then already I was playing for a few years but I never heard any jazz. And then one day a guy who was a journalist and a writer, he was a journalist, he talked to me and said, “Hey, you ever hear the jazz music?” And I say, “What is that?” He said, “Come with me, I’m going to play something for you.” And he played for me a vinyl, you know it was a compilation of recordings from the 40s from Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. That was the very first thing I ever heard about. And I will never forget that moment. It’s still in my mind for sixty years or more— I’m sorry — less than sixty years because I was already like 18, 19 years old and I never heard any jazz before at all. And that thing impressed me so much that I couldn’t speak. You know I was — you know I said oh my Lord, what the heck those people are playing? This is what you call jazz? He said yes, yes. Man, I wanted to learn that. I don’t know how or when but I want to learn that. And I’m still on a mission after so many years. I’m still on a mission. And we’re never going to reach the end in terms of learning. I believe you know it’s our mission to keep listening, paying attention, investigating, and keep trying to improve what you do. If you believe that you have reached some point already it’s like the famous phrase “sleeping in your laurels” you know. And that’s not smart. That’s not smart. Because that means the end of your growing process. And the growing process is something that you don’t have any end, only with your death.
